sections.title: Taxonomy
sections.text: The name accepted by Index Fungorum is Tremella mesenterica Retz. (1769), in the family Tremellaceae and order Tremellales. The UK Natural History Museum and other databases list Tremella lutescens as a synonym. It is a gelatinous basidiomycete without a distinct cap or stem.

sections.title: Morphology and hymenium
sections.text: The sessile fruit body forms an irregular, lobed, often brain-like mass, usually a few centimetres across and sometimes up to about 10 cm. It ranges from sulfur yellow to vivid yellow-orange. When wet it is soft, gelatinous, sometimes translucent and glossy; as it dries it shrinks and becomes duller and leathery, then swells again after rehydration. A cut section shows continuous gelatinous flesh, with no stem, gills or pores. The hymenium covers the exposed folds and ridges, so the underside view also has a folded surface rather than gills.

sections.title: Ecology
sections.text: Yellow brain occurs on dead branches and wood, often from broadleaved trees. It is mycoparasitic: the visible wood is generally being decomposed by a host fungus, especially a crust fungus in the genus Peniophora, rather than directly consumed by Tremella. Zugmaier et al. experimentally demonstrated in-vivo parasitism of Peniophora laeta. Fruiting bodies can appear throughout the year in temperate climates and are most conspicuous when saturated with water.

sections.title: Identification and caution
sections.text: The yellow-orange, lobed, gelatinous form is characteristic, but several jelly fungi can look similar. A photograph alone may not confirm the species; ecological clues, including broadleaf wood and possible Peniophora, and mycological examination are useful. This entry is not a guide to identifying or eating a wild collection.

traits: Sessile, irregularly lobed, often brain-like fruit body, usually a few centimetres across.
Sulfur yellow to yellow-orange; soft, gelatinous and sometimes translucent when wet, duller and shrunken when dry.
Uniform gelatinous flesh in section; no cap, stem, gills or pores.
The fertile hymenium covers the exposed folds; the underside is also folded and has no gills.
Mycoparasite of wood-inhabiting fungi, especially Peniophora; it appears on dead wood but does not itself cause wood decay.
May fruit throughout the year; the masses are most conspicuous when rehydrated.
safetyNote: Taxonomic and ecological reference. This entry cannot identify a wild collection or assess edibility; do not eat a specimen based on this entry.
